name: Cold-pressed oils / olive oil

image.caption: Salt, olive oil, vinegar - Hellenic Republic

lead: Cold-pressed oils, most prominently extra virgin olive oil, are extracted mechanically without heat or solvents. People in looksmaxxing and diet circles use them in place of refined seed oils, linking them to healthier skin and general health.

The oil is rich in oleic acid and polyphenols. In the US the FDA allows a qualified health claim that limited and not conclusive evidence suggests about two tablespoons daily may reduce coronary heart disease risk when replacing saturated fat; effects on appearance have not been established.

paras: People use extra virgin olive oil for dressings, finishing and low-to-medium heat cooking, and swap it in for seed oils. Because its polyphenols are sensitive to heat, light and oxygen, it is usually stored dark and cool.
Few direct risks are reported. Documented concerns involve fraud and mislabelling in the olive oil market, and the FDA claim is described as limited and not conclusive.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers use extra virgin olive oil and other cold-pressed oils in place of refined seed oils, citing skin and general health. Swapping oils changes fatty acid and polyphenol intake, which is the route people credit for healthier skin. Olive oil has regulator-qualified heart-health claims; appearance effects have not been tested.

lead: Cold-pressed oils, most prominently extra virgin olive oil, are edible oils extracted mechanically without heat or chemical solvents. In looksmaxxing and wider diet-culture discussion they are used as the cooking and finishing fat in place of refined seed oils, with followers hoping for healthier skin, a leaner physique and better general health, and some also use olive oil as a calorie-dense way to add food intake while bulking [1][2][3].

Extra virgin olive oil is the top grade under International Olive Council standards, requiring cold mechanical extraction and free acidity of no more than 0.8 percent [1]. In the US the FDA allows a qualified health claim that limited and not conclusive evidence suggests about two tablespoons daily may reduce coronary heart disease risk when replacing saturated fat [1].

Research on olive oil centres on cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes: an umbrella review of vegetable oils found that virgin olive oil, canola and rice bran oils were associated with lower total and LDL cholesterol, and polyphenol reviews describe antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [4][5]. A small randomized forearm study examined olive oil applied directly to adult skin and its effect on the skin barrier [6].
infobox: Not examined in the sources reviewed

paras: Virgin oils are made by mechanical means only. Cold pressed generally means the oil was not heated above about 27 degrees Celsius, though the EU reserves that term for oil that is physically pressed rather than centrifuged, and the phrase first cold pressed has no reliable international definition [1].
Production involves crushing olives, stirring the paste, separating oil by pressing or centrifuge, and optional filtering. Refined and pomace oils involve chemical processing or solvents [1].

Olive oil is mostly monounsaturated oleic acid, with smaller amounts of linoleic and palmitic acid. Polyphenols make up about 0.5 percent and give the bitter, peppery taste but decline with heat, light and oxygen [1].

In 2011 the European Food Safety Authority supported claims that olive polyphenols protect blood lipids from oxidation and that replacing saturated fat with oleic acid helps maintain normal LDL cholesterol, but said cause and effect was not established for triglycerides, HDL cholesterol or blood glucose [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and diet communities
paras: On looksmax.org, olive oil appears mainly in diet threads, for example a member asking how to use it to add calories for bulking; a reply notes that extra calories from any source add body fat that can be lost later in a deficit [2]. T Nation forum members have likewise discussed olive oil as a calorie source for athletes struggling to eat enough, and as a preferred cold-pressed oil for low-heat cooking [3]. Proponents of seed-oil avoidance regard cold-pressed olive oil as a cleaner alternative, a view not directly tested for appearance outcomes.

Ancient Greeks rubbed oil on the body during exercise, and cosmetic use began in the 7th century BC [1]. In a 2013 randomized study of 19 adult volunteers, researchers compared olive oil and sunflower seed oil applied to forearm skin and measured the effect on skin barrier properties; the study was framed around neonatal skin care practice [6].

Journalist Tom Mueller's reporting and 2011 book Extra Virginity alleged widespread mislabelling of extra virgin oil, and authorities have conducted enforcement operations in Italy and Spain, including arrests in 2008 and 2012. In July 2024 the EU reported record olive oil fraud cases [1].

An umbrella review of 48 studies and 206 meta-analyses reported that virgin olive oil was among the monounsaturated-rich oils associated with lower total cholesterol and LDL concentrations, with certainty ranging from moderate to very low [4]. A meta-analysis of olive oil consumption examined cardiovascular disease, cancer, type 2 diabetes and mortality outcomes [7], and the PREDIMED and CORDIOPREV trials tested Mediterranean diets rich in extra virgin olive oil in cardiovascular settings [8][9]. A randomized comparison of coconut oil, olive oil and butter measured blood lipids and cardiovascular risk factors in healthy adults [10]. For appearance, a 2013 forearm trial examined olive oil on the adult skin barrier [6]. No studies were found on cold-pressed oils as a seed-oil replacement for appearance outcomes.
